The best way to build a chicken wire compost bin is a staked cylinder design, which takes about 30 minutes to assemble for around $30 to $45. Unlike a freestanding wire ring that sags over time, driving four metal T-posts into the ground keeps the structure rigid and makes it easy to unhook and unwrap when you are ready to turn or harvest your pile. What You'll Need

• Tools: Heavy-duty leather work gloves, tin snips or wire cutters, pliers, and a post driver or heavy mallet.
• Materials: One 12.5-foot length of 36-inch-tall galvanized chicken wire (1-inch hex mesh), four 4-foot metal T-posts or U-posts, and heavy-duty UV-resistant zip ties or 16-gauge bailing wire.
• Optional Upgrade: Swap standard chicken wire for 1/4-inch galvanized hardware cloth if you plan to compost food scraps in an area with mice, rats, or chipmunks. Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Clear the site. Pick a flat, well-drained spot at least 2 feet away from fences or wooden structures to prevent rot, and clear away grass or weeds. Laying down a layer of plain cardboard helps block weeds from growing up into your pile.
2. Cut and hem the wire. Unroll 12.5 feet of wire (this forms a 4-foot-wide circle, the ideal volume for hot composting) and snip it free. Fold the cut ends back 2 to 3 inches against themselves and crimp them flat with pliers so no sharp points stick out.
3. Drive the support posts. Space your four posts evenly in a 4-foot circle, leaving about 12 inches of the bottom end driven firmly into the ground so they do not lean outward under the weight of wet compost.
4. Wrap the wire mesh. Stand the wire upright around the outside of the posts so the posts brace the mesh from the inside. Overlap the two folded ends by about 4 to 6 inches.
5. Fasten and create a gate. Secure the wire to three of the posts using zip ties or twisted bailing wire. On the fourth post where the ends overlap, use reusable heavy-duty clips, bungee cords, or twisted wire loops so you can easily unlatch and peel back the wall to shovel out finished compost. Quick Tips for Success

• Mind your ratio. Keep the bin odor-free by layering two parts dry "browns" (shredded leaves, straw, cardboard) for every one part wet "greens" (grass clippings, vegetable scraps).
• Skip meat and dairy. Because wire bins are open to the air, stick strictly to plant matter, eggshells, and coffee grounds so you do not attract raccoons, skunks, or neighborhood dogs. About Tomatoes

Originating in South America, the tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) has the distinction of being one of North America’s favorite garden vegetables. Tomatoes come in hundreds of varieties, from large, ribbed “beefsteak” types to small “cherry” and “pear-shaped” tomatoes and in an array of colors and shapes.

With over 75 outstanding varieties from Seed Savers Exchange to choose from, determining which tomatoes to grow can be a tough decision! Fortunately, tomatoes can be categorized in several ways to help you narrow down a vast selection to the varieties right for you and your garden.

Four Types of Tomatoes You Need in Your Garden
1. Beefsteak

Two large red 'Dester' tomatoes on a smooth granite surface
Popular beefsteak variety: ‘Dester’
Large, meaty, great for burgers and sandwiches
Our picks: Brandywine (Sudduth’s Strain), Dester

2. Slicer

Three deep red-purple 'Cherokee Purple' tomatoes arranged on a wood cutting board.
Popular slicer variety: ‘Cherokee Purple’
Great for slicing and canning
Our picks: Cherokee Purple, Green Zebra

3. Cherry

Popular cherry variety: ‘Igleheart Yellow Cherry’
Great for snacking and salads
Our picks: Black Cherry, Igleheart Yellow Cherry

4. Paste/Roma

Three red 'Amish Paste' tomatoes and four tomato slices on a countertop
Popular paste variety: ‘Amish Paste’
Great for sauces, salsa, baking, and canning
Our picks: Amish Paste, Martino’s Roma
Shop all paste tomato seeds

Determinate vs. Indeterminate Tomatoes
Tomato plants can be either determinate or indeterminate.

A cluster of six small red 'Martino's Roma' tomatoes attached to a vine next to three more tomatoes in a wooden bowl
Determinate: ‘Martino’s Roma’
Determinate tomato plants will produce tomatoes that all ripen around the same time.

Typically small and compact
Short harvest period
Ideal for canning
Shop all determinate tomato seeds

Three red and yellow-splashed 'Peg O' My Heart' tomatoes stacked on top of each other against a stone background
Indeterminate: ‘Peg O’ My Heart’ — NEW!
Indeterminate tomato plants will continue producing new growth and new fruits until killed by frost

Typically large and sprawling, need support
Harvest period of 2-3 months
Yields usually higher than determinate varieties
Typically later to mature than determinate varieties
Shop all indeterminate tomato seeds

Tomato Earliness
Different varieties mature at various times in the season, but can generally be categorized into early, mid-season, and late.

Early: <69 days

Five oblong yellow and green 'Willie's Garden' tomatoes and a few yellow tomato slices in a wooden bowl
‘Willie’s Garden,’ 65 days from transplant
Our picks: ‘Council Bluffs Heirloom,’ ‘Willie’s Garden,’ ‘Mexico Midget,’ and ‘Baker Family Heirloom’

Mid-Season: 70-84 days

Two large red 'Italian Heirloom' tomatoes with splashes of yellow
‘Italian Heirloom,’ 70-80 days from transplant
Our picks: ‘Oma’s Orange,’ ‘Chocolate Cherry,’ ‘Italian Heirloom’

Late: 85+ days

Three dark red-purple 'Paul Robeson' tomatoes with two tomato slices
‘Paul Robeson,’ 80-90 days from transplant
Our picks: ‘Peg O’ My Heart,’ ‘Paul Robeson,’ ‘Mortgage Lifter (Halladay’s)’

Need to get a new chain for the chainsaw. The other one is worn and isn't cutting very well any more. Make sure to get the proper size (M66) . I also need to get some new chainsaw oil to lubricate the chain.

Beefsteak tomatoes experienced slow growth due to drought. We set up irrigation on timers after the 3rd week. But, it did stunt the growth of the plants early on. Next year, set up the irrigation in advance before growing season starts. Also, do daily watering via hose or watering can.

Need to come up with a better way to trellis the peas. As the plants grow it adds a lot of weight to the twine trellis. This leads to it breaking towards the end of the season. Next year let's try 2 metal T-posts with some chicken wire stretched across it with steel wire. This will support the full weight of multiple plants much better.
